'''''Leucophyllum frutescens''''' is an [[evergreen]] [[shrub]] in the [[Scrophularia|figwort]] family, [[Scrophulariaceae]], native to the U.S. state of [[Texas]], where it is the official "State Native Shrub of Texas",<ref name=HCR>{{cite web | url=https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/79r/billtext/html/HC00071F.HTM | title=H.C.R. 71, 2005}}</ref> and to the states of [[Coahuila]], [[Nuevo León]], and [[Tamaulipas]] in northern Mexico. Although commonly known as '''Texas sage''', it is not a true sage and is distinct from the genus ''[[Salvia]]''. The species is also called '''Texas Ranger''', '''Texas rain sage''', '''''cenizo''''', '''Texas silverleaf''', '''Texas barometerbush''', '''ash-bush''', '''wild lilac''', '''purple sage''', '''''senisa''''', '''''cenicilla''''', '''''palo cenizo''''', or '''''hierba del cenizo'''''.

==Description==
The solitary axillary flowers are bell- or funnel-shaped, with five lobes and two lips. This species is found in rocky, [[calcareous]] soils.<ref name="A&M">{{cite web |url=https://aggie-horticulture.tamu.edu/ornamentals/nativeshrubs/leucophyllumfrutes.htm |title=Texas Sage, Texas Ranger, Texas Rain Sage, Cenizo, Texas Silverleaf, Ash-bush, Wild Lilac, Purple Sage, Senisa, Cenicilla, Palo Cenizo, Hierba del Cenizo ''Leucophyllum frutescens'' |work=Benny Simpson's Texas Native Shrubs |publisher=Texas A&M University |access-date=2010-04-11}}</ref> 

==Cultivation==
Due to its abundant purple flowers, Texas sage is a popular [[ornamental plant]], commonly used for edge and area plantings in warmer and drier areas. It requires minimal water, is easily shaped into [[hedge]]s, and blooms over the entire surface. It is available in a variety of [[cultivar]]s, including 'Green Cloud', 'White Cloud', 'Compacta', 'Convent', and 'Bert-Star'.<ref name="Irish">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AyWkIsLDca8C |title=Trees and Shrubs for the Southwest: Woody Plants for Arid Gardens |first=Mary |last=Irish |publisher=Timber Press |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-88192-905-8 |pages=221–223}}</ref>

==Ecology==
''Leucophyllum frutescens'' is a host plant for the [[caterpillar]]s of the theona checkerspot (''[[Chlosyne theona]]'')<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.butterfliesandmoths.org/species?l=1707 |title=Theona Checkerspot ''Chlosyne theona'' (Ménétriés, 1855) |publisher=Butterflies and Moths of North America |access-date=2010-08-22 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120723031916/http://www.butterfliesandmoths.org/species/Chlosyne-theona |archive-date=2012-07-23 |url-status=dead}}</ref> and calleta silkmoth
(''[[Eupackardia calleta]]'').<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.butterfliesandmoths.org/species?l=3287 |title=Calleta silkmoth ''Eupackardia calleta'' (Westwood, 1853) |publisher=Butterflies and Moths of North America |access-date=2010-08-22 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080531151544/http://www.butterfliesandmoths.org/species?l=3287 |archive-date=2008-05-31}}</ref>

== Barometer bush ==
[[File:Ornamental Texas sage in bloom.jpg|thumb|right|Ornamental Texas sage in bloom]]
[[File:Texas Sage -- Leucophyllum frutescens.jpg|thumb|Texas sage]]Texas sage is nicknamed the "barometer bush" due to a commonly held belief that it can predict the rain. According to folklore, the plant goes into bloom in anticipation of upcoming rain. It appears that the plant sometimes blooms because of humidity or low atmospheric pressure, which can occur before or after rain.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jimenez |first=Elisabeth |date=2023-12-13 |title=Texas Sage Is the Weatherman of the Plant World |url=https://www.texasmonthly.com/travel/texas-sage-weatherman-of-plant-world/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20231220172709/https://www.texasmonthly.com/travel/texas-sage-weatherman-of-plant-world/ |archive-date=2023-12-20 |access-date=2025-01-03 |website=Texas Monthly |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Ottensman |first=Nick |date=2023-05-30 |title=Growing Rugged Texas Sage in the Coastal Bend |url=https://www.thebendmag.com/growing-rugged-texas-sage-in-the-coastal-bend/ |access-date=2025-01-03 |website=The Bend Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Holley |first=Lydia |date=2022-08-15 |title=Waiting on the Barometer Bush to Bloom |url=https://txmg.org/hendersonmg/publicity/waiting-on-the-barometer-bush-to-bloom/ |access-date=2025-01-03 |website=HCMGA |language=en-US}}</ref>
